## Overview 

- Extrahepatic biliary tumors are **rare** but aggressive neoplasms, predominantly cholangiocarcinoma.  
- Management is complex and requires an **experienced multidisciplinary team**.

---

## Chapter scope:

- Epidemiology & risk factors  
- Histopathology & molecular profiling  
- Clinical presentation & diagnostic workup  
- Preoperative staging & resectability assessment  
- Biliary drainage & portal vein embolization  
- Surgical resection techniques  
- Adjuvant & palliative therapies  
- Outcomes

---

## Epidemiology — Subtypes & Incidence {.smaller}

**Cholangiocarcinoma = 3% of all digestive cancers**

| Subtype | Abbreviation | Proportion |
|---|---|---|
| Intrahepatic | ICC | 20% |
| Perihilar (Klatskin) | HC | 50–60% |
| Distal | DC | 20–30% |

- Equal sex distribution  
- Blacks & whites: rising incidence; Hispanics: stable  
- **~20% diagnosed before age 60**; largest rise in ages **18–44**

:::{.callout}
EHC incidence **increased 20%** from 1973–2012  
(1.6 → 2.3 per 100,000 individuals)  
~**2,500 new cases/year** in the United States
:::
---

## Risk Factors {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Cholestatic / Structural**

- Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
- Choledochal cysts
- Recurrent pyogenic cholangiohepatitis
- Hepatolithiasis
- Biliary parasites
- Caroli disease / congenital hepatic fibrosis

*Common pathway: cholestasis + chronic inflammation*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Metabolic / Other**

- Type 2 diabetes  
  (RR 1.60 cholangiocarcinoma; RR 1.63 EHC; RR 1.97 ICC)
- Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
- Obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension
- Lynch syndrome *(rare genetic disorder)*
- Bile salt transporter protein gene defects
:::
:::

::: {.callout}
*Most Western cases: **sporadic**, no obvious risk factor*
:::


---

## Tumor Location {.smaller}

**EHC arises from first-order bile ducts → ampulla of Vater**

- **Perihilar (Klatskin) HC:** first described 1965; arises in right/left hepatic duct or confluence  
- **Distal DC:** arises in common bile duct distal to cystic duct takeoff

:::{.callout}
Any extrahepatic biliary strictures are **highly suggestive of malignancy**  
Brush/biopsy: high specificity but **limited sensitivity**  
"Malignant masquerade" (benign strictures can mimic cancer)
:::

**Benign strictures (Causes)**

- Autoimmune cholangiopathy
- Autoimmune pancreatitis
- Choleodcholithiasis
- PSC


---

## Tumor Histopathology

**Dominant histology:** Adenocarcinoma **>75%**

**Precancerous lesions:**

- Biliary intraepithelial neoplasia (BilIN)
- Intraductal papillary neoplasm of the biliary tract (IPNB)
- Intraductal tubular papillary neoplasm (ITPN)
- Mucinous cystic neoplasm

---

## Adenocarcinoma Subtypes {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Sclerosing**  

- Most common.  
- Thickened bile duct walls with proximal dilation.  
- Dense fibrous stroma.  
- Worst prognosis.
:::

:::{.column width="30%"}
**Nodular**  

- Discrete mass-like lesion.  
- Mixed features.  
- Intermediate prognosis.
:::


:::{.column width="30%"}
**Papillary**  

- Up to **25%** of EHCs.  
- Expands duct lumen.  
- **Best prognosis** among subtypes.  
- Friable — can cause intermittent jaundice.
:::
:::


:::{.callout}

**Immunohistochemical markers of EHC:**  

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- Mucin
- MUC5AC
- MUC6
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

- S100P
- SMAD4 loss
- BAP1
:::
:::
:::
---

## Molecular Profiling {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="30%"}
**Perihilar HC**

- KRAS mutations: **55%**
- TP53 mutations: **40%**
- SMAD4
- MMR deficiency: **~5%** (immunotherapy potential)
:::
:::{.column width="30%"}
**Extrahepatic (EHC)**

- PRKACA / PRKACB fusions
- Mutations in ELF3, ERBB2, ARID1B
- HER2 amplification: **~20%** of EHC

*Targetable mutations: **rare** in EHC*
:::


:::{.column width="30%"}
**Intrahepatic (ICC)**

- IDH mutations
- EPHA2 mutations
- BAP1 mutations
- FGFR2 fusions *(targetable)*

*Richer targetable landscape in ICC than EHC*
:::
:::

:::{.callout}
ALK and TP53 mutations → worse prognosis in EHC  
Molecular testing of EHC is **recommended**.
:::

---

## Clinical Presentation {.smaller}

**Determined by tumor size and location**

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma (HC)**

- Jaundice in **90%** at presentation
- Early HC: unilateral obstruction → no jaundice  
  → isolated ↑ ALP may be the only clue
- Papillary hilar tumors: **intermittent jaundice** (ball-valve effect)
- Jaundice often a **late finding** in HC
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Distal Cholangiocarcinoma (DC)**

- Presentation similar to periampullary tumors
- Classic **painless obstructive jaundice**
- Earlier detection due to complete obstruction
:::
:::


---

## Clinical Presentation {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Systemic symptoms:** 

- abdominal pain 
- weight loss 
- nausea 
- pruritus 
- acholic stools 
- choluria
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Labs:** 

- ↑ Total bilirubin 
- ↑ Direct bilirubin
- ↑ ALP 
- ↑ GGT  
:::
:::
**Tumor markers:** 

- CA19-9 (often markedly ↑ in jaundice) 
- CEA

---

## Bilirubin Levels & Differential Diagnosis {.smaller}


**Bilirubin as a diagnostic clue:**

| Level | Suggests |
|---|---|
| **> 10 mg/dL** | Malignant obstruction |
| **2–4 mg/dL** | Choledocholithiasis (significant overlap) |


**Cholangitis at presentation:**

- Rare without prior biliary manipulation (no bactibilia in uninstrumented tree)
- **100% bactibilia** after biliary instrumentation compromising the sphincter of Oddi

---

## Bilirubin Levels & Differential Diagnosis 

**Physical examination:**

- Jaundice is the dominant finding
- Enlarged gallbladder → obstruction **distal** to or involving cystic duct
- Collapsed gallbladder → **proximal** biliary obstruction (HC)
- Portal hypertension signs in long-standing disease

---

## Differential Diagnosis of Hilar Strictures {.smaller}

**10–15% of patients with hilar strictures do NOT have cholangiocarcinoma**

| Alternative Diagnosis | Distinguishing Features |
|---|---|
| Gallbladder carcinoma | Thickened irregular GB wall; infiltration segments IV/V; right portal pedicle involvement; cystic duct occlusion on ERCP |
| Mirizzi syndrome | Stone at cystic duct; no mass lesion |


---

## Differential Diagnosis of Hilar Strictures {.smaller}

| Alternative Diagnosis | Distinguishing Features |
|---|---|
| Autoimmune cholangitis | Smooth tapered stricture; serum IgG4 ↑; steroid response |
| Lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis | Associated pancreatic changes |
| PSC | Known history; multifocal strictures |
| Granulomatous disease | Systemic features; tissue diagnosis |

:::{.callout}
Benign strictures account for **10–15%** of resected specimens — surgical resection may be required for definitive diagnosis
:::

---

## Diagnostic Imaging — Ultrasound {.smaller}

**Abdominal ultrasound: first-line evaluation**

- Noninvasive and cost-effective
- Findings often **nonspecific**: biliary dilatation
- Low sensitivity for level of obstruction

:::{.callout}
**Duplex Ultrasonography** (in experienced hands):

- Accurately predicts **vascular involvement**
- Portal vein invasion prediction: **93% sensitivity, 99% specificity, 97% PPV** (MSKCC, n=63)
- Particularly useful when vascular involvement is questionable
:::

With widespread multiphasic CT and MRI/MRCP availability, ultrasound is less used preoperatively but remains a **valuable adjunct**

---

## Diagnostic Imaging — CT & MRI {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Multidetector Multiphasic CT**

- 1 mm thin cuts: arterial + portal venous phases
- Evaluates:
  - Level of biliary obstruction
  - Vascular involvement (PV, HA)
  - Hepatic lobar atrophy
  - Metastatic disease
  - 3D CT arteriography in single session
- **Preferred:** Quadruple-phase liver CT + chest/pelvis
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**MRI with MRCP**

- Depicts level of obstruction & biliary anatomy
- Identifies obstructed/isolated ducts not seen on ERCP/PTC
- Assesses vascular involvement, lobar atrophy, nodal/distant disease
- **Has replaced direct cholangiography** for initial staging
- Comparable to CT for assessing resectability
:::
:::

:::{.callout}
*Imaging should be performed **before biliary decompression** to assess resectability — stents cause inflammation and distortion*
:::

---

## Diagnostic Imaging — PET/CT & Direct Cholangiography {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**PET/CT (18FDG-PET)**

Role is **limited** in EHC

| Application | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|---|---|---|
| Primary tumor | 91.7% | 51.3% |
| Lymph node | 88.4% | 69.1% |
| Distant mets | 85.4% | 89.7% |
| Relapse after resection | 90.1% | 83.5% |

Best as a **problem-solving tool** for equivocal findings; routine preoperative use unproven
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**ERCP / PTC (Direct Cholangiography)**

- Sensitivity/specificity ~**70–75%** for tissue diagnosis
- Allows biopsy + biliary drainage
- **No longer needed for staging** (replaced by MRCP)
- Now limited to: biliary decompression + tissue sampling
- Tissue diagnosis **not mandatory** before resection when clinical suspicion is high
:::
:::

---

## Preoperative Evaluation — Goals {.smaller}

**When EHC is suspected, focus on:**

1. **Resectability assessment**
2. **Hepatic reserve evaluation**
3. **Overall performance status**

:::{.callout}
Contraindications to surgery: 

- portal hypertension
- cirrhosis 
- poor performance status
- metastatic disease
:::

---

## Preoperative Evaluation {.smaller}

**Resectability: 4 key criteria (Table 51A.1)**

| Criterion | Assessment |
|---|---|
| 1. Biliary tree involvement | Cross-sectional imaging (extent of ductal involvement) |
| 2. Lobar atrophy | CT/MRI (shrunken, hypoperfused lobe with crowded ducts) |
| 3. Vascular involvement | PV contour change/occlusion; hepatic artery encasement |
| 4. Metastatic disease | CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; diagnostic laparoscopy |

---

## Criteria for Non-Resectability in HC {.smaller}

| Category | Criteria |
|---|---|
| **Patient Factors** | Medically unfit for major operation · Cirrhosis with portal hypertension |
| **Local Tumor Extent** | Bilateral hepatic duct involvement to secondary radicles · Main portal vein encasement/occlusion · Ipsilateral PV branch encasement + contralateral atrophy · Bilateral secondary radicle involvement + contralateral atrophy |
| **Distant Spread** | Positive nodes **outside** hepatoduodenal ligament · Metastases to liver, lung, peritoneum, or other distant organs |

:::{.callout}
**Lobar atrophy** = critical finding:  
- Long-standing biliary obstruction → moderate atrophy  
- Concomitant ipsilateral PV compromise → **rapid, severe atrophy**
:::

---

## Pretreatment Biliary Drainage {.smaller}

**Key principle: selective, appropriately planned drainage of the future liver remnant (FLR)**


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Immediate decompression required for:**

- Cholangitic patients
- Jaundiced patients needing systemic chemotherapy
- Hyperbilirubinemia-induced malnutrition
- Hepatic insufficiency
- Jaundiced patients undergoing PVE
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**HC vs DC drainage:**

- DC: **single** catheter/stent sufficient
- HC: **multiple** biliary drainage catheters of the FLR often necessary
:::
:::

**Internal drainage preferred** over external — prevents bile loss, malabsorption, dehydration, and intestinal barrier dysfunction

---

## Biliary Drainage — FLR Volume Thresholds {.smaller}

**Kennedy et al. (MSKCC, n=60) — Impact of FLR on outcomes:**

| FLR | Drainage | Operative Mortality | Hepatic Insufficiency |
|---|---|---|---|
| < 30% | Not drained | **33%** | 33% |
| < 30% | Drained | 0% | 0% |
| ≥ 30% | Not drained | 0% | 0% |
| ≥ 30% | Drained | 9.1% | 0% |

:::{.callout}
**Conclusion:**

- FLR ≥ 30–40%: surgery without drainage is safe; drainage may introduce risk
- FLR < 30–40%: preoperative biliary drainage **improves outcomes**
- Large FLR (>50%): drainage associated with **increased mortality** (12% vs 0%)
:::

---

## Biliary Drainage — Approach Comparison {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="30%"}

**EBD (Endoscopic)**

✅ No external drains  
❌ Stent misplacement common  
❌ High cholangitis risk when multiple ducts opacified but not drained  
❌ Up to 50% require crossover to PTBD
:::

:::{.column width="30%"}
**PTBD (Percutaneous)**

✅ Precise FLR catheter placement  
✅ Delineates biliary tumor extent  
✅ Internal drainage above ampulla → better patency  
✅ Preferred by authors  
❌ Catheter discomfort  
❌ Rare tract seeding (associated with distant mets)
:::

:::{.column width="30%"}
**ENBD (Nasobiliary)**

✅ Lower biliary re-intervention rate (OR 0.26)  
❌ Significant patient discomfort  
❌ E-POD study: no advantage over EBD as initial approach  
Used mainly in **Asian centers**
:::
:::

---

## Biliary Drainage — Approach Comparison

:::{.callout}
RCT (Netherlands, n=54): stopped early; PTBD showed higher mortality vs EBD (41% vs 11%) — but significant crossover and type I error concerns. PTBD remains acceptable and authors' preferred approach.
:::

---

## Portal Vein Embolization (PVE) {.smaller}

**Goal: induce hypertrophy of the planned FLR before major hepatectomy**

**Indications:**

- FLR < 25% (normal liver)
- FLR < 30% (chemotherapy-induced liver toxicity)
- FLR < 40% (cirrhosis / underlying liver dysfunction)
- **Authors' threshold: FLR < 40%** (given cholestatic liver failure + neoadjuvant chemo needs)

**Approach:** Percutaneous transhepatic (most common) — no general anesthesia required

:::{.callout}
**Outcomes of PVE:**

- FLR increase: absolute **8–37.9%**
- Morbidity: 2–2.5% · Mortality: 0.1%
- **Kinetic Growth Rate (KGR)** = % hypertrophy / weeks since PVE  
  KGR > 2.66%/week → no postoperative liver insufficiency (n=153)
:::

---

## Preoperative Staging Systems

**Bismuth-Corlette Classification**

| Type | Extent |
|---|---|
| I | Distal to biliary confluence |
| II | Involves confluence |
| IIIA | Extends to right hepatic duct |
| IIIB | Extends to left hepatic duct |
| IV | Involves confluence + bilateral ducts |

❌ Does not describe vascular involvement, resectability, or prognosis

---

## Preoperative Staging Systems {.smaller}

**MSKCC T-Staging (Jarnagin et al.)**

*Predicts resectability & R0 likelihood*

| Stage | Criteria |
|---|---|
| T1 | Confluence ± unilateral 2nd-order radicles |
| T2 | T1 + ipsilateral PV involvement ± ipsilateral lobar atrophy |
| T3 | T1 + contralateral PV involvement or contralateral lobar atrophy; or bilateral PV involvement |

✅ Significantly associated with overall survival

---

## AJCC Staging (8th Edition) — Perihilar Bile Duct {.smaller}

**Primary Tumor (T)**

| T | Description |
|---|---|
| T1 | Confined to bile duct wall (muscle/fibrous tissue) |
| T2a | Invades periductal adipose tissue |
| T2b | Invades adjacent hepatic parenchyma |
| T3 | Invades unilateral portal vein or hepatic artery branches |
| T4 | Invades main PV bilaterally, common HA, or unilateral 2nd-order radicles + contralateral PV/HA |


---

## AJCC Staging (8th Edition) — Perihilar Bile Duct {.smaller}

**Regional Nodes (N)**

| N | Description |
|---|---|
| N0 | No regional nodal metastasis |
| N1 | 1–3 positive hilar/CBD/HA/portal vein nodes |
| N2 | ≥4 positive nodes |

---

## AJCC Staging (8th Edition) — Perihilar Bile Duct {.smaller}


**Prognostic Groups**

| Stage | T | N | M |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Tis | N0 | M0 |
| I | T1 | N0 | M0 |
| II | T2a/b | N0 | M0 |
| IIIA | T3 | N0 | M0 |
| IIIB | T4 | N0 | M0 |
| IIIC | Any T | N1 | M0 |
| IVA | Any T | N2 | M0 |
| IVB | Any T | Any N | M1 |

*Based on pathologic findings — **no utility in preoperative management***

---

## Diagnostic Laparoscopy {.smaller}

**Despite improved imaging, up to 50% of patients have unresectable disease at exploration**

:::{.callout}
**Value of staging laparoscopy:**

- Avoids non-therapeutic laparotomy in **~25%** of patients
- UK retrospective review (2010–2015): **27.2%** spared futile laparotomy
- MSKCC review (n=56 radiographically resectable): **25% (14 patients)** found to have metastatic disease
- Yield increases to **36%** in T2/T3 tumors
:::


---

## Diagnostic Laparoscopy {.smaller}

:::{.callout}
**Particularly indicated in:**  

Locally advanced, potentially resectable HC (Blumgart T2/T3)
:::

Findings at laparoscopy that preclude resection:
- Intrahepatic metastases
- Peritoneal implants
- Distant lymph node metastases

---

## Management Algorithm for Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma {.smaller}

```
Hilar biliary obstruction
│
├── Quadruple-phase liver CT + chest/pelvis (MRCP, duplex US)
│
├── Selective biliary decompression* (*mandatory if cholangitis)
│
├─ RESECTABLE (Blumgart T1–2)
│   ├── FLR > 40% → Resect
│   └── FLR < 40% → PVE + biliary decompression → Resect
│
├─ LOCALLY ADVANCED (Blumgart T3)
│   ├── Biliary decompression
│   ├── Neoadjuvant therapy (systemic ± XRT)
│   ├── Restage + volumetrics + selective PVE
│   ├── Resectable → Resect
│   └── Unresectable → Definitive systemic therapy (Gem/Cis)
│
└─ METASTATIC
    └── Biliary stent → Definitive systemic therapy
```

---

## Resection of Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma — Principles {.smaller}

**Primary objective: complete tumor extirpation (R0) + biliary-enteric continuity**

:::{.callout}
**Operative approach by location:**

- **Distal bile duct:** pancreaticoduodenectomy
- **Hilar tumors:** major hepatectomy + en bloc bile duct excision ± caudate lobectomy
:::

**Why caudate lobectomy?**

- Main caudate lobe ducts drain into the **left hepatic duct**
- Left hepatic duct tumors frequently involve caudate ducts
- Dilated caudate duct on pre-drainage imaging = tumor involvement

---

## Resection of Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma — Principles {.smaller}

**Margin status and survival:**

| Margin | Median DSS |
|---|---|
| Wide negative (R0) | **56 months** |
| Narrow negative | 38 months |
| Positive (R1) | 32 months |
| Locally advanced (explored, unresectable) | 16 months |

---

## Resection — Key Technical Steps {.smaller}

**Access:** Right subcostal incision ± proximal xiphoid extension ("hockey stick") or midline

1. **Inspect peritoneal cavity** — rule out metastatic disease; frozen section of suspicious nodes
2. **Intraoperative ultrasound** — unsuspected hepatic masses
3. **Assess vascular involvement** — critical for planned left-sided resections (right hepatic artery)
4. **Transect common bile duct** above duodenum → turn upward

---

## Resection — Key Technical Steps {.smaller}

5. **Expose liver hilum** — take down gallbladder, lower hilar plate (incise Glisson capsule at segment IV base)
6. **Expose left hepatic duct** — divide segment IV/left lateral segment bridge of liver
7. **Dissect portal vein** — develop plane between bile duct tumor and portal vein
8. **Assess proximal extent** — palpation ± biopsy
9. If hepatectomy needed: ligate/transect ipsilateral PV branch and hepatic artery; divide ipsilateral hepatic vein before parenchymal transection

---

## Biliary-Enteric Reconstruction {.smaller}

**Hepaticojejunostomy to Roux-en-Y loop of jejunum** (retrocolic fashion, end-to-side)

:::{.callout}
**Managing multiple duct orifices after tumor removal:**

- Right anterior and posterior sectoral ducts may become discontinuous
- Caudate ducts may separate from left hepatic duct
- Approximate adjacent duct sidewalls with sutures → treat as single duct
- Usually achievable with ≤ 2–3 separate anastomoses
:::

---

## Biliary-Enteric Reconstruction {.smaller}

**Suture technique for multiple disconnected ducts:**

1. Place entire **anterior row** of sutures to all exposed ducts
2. Place entire **posterior row** to ducts and jejunum
3. Railroad jejunum on posterior sutures
4. Tie posterior layer first (back wall flush with jejunum)
5. Pass anterior sutures sequentially through anterior jejunal wall

**CVP:** Keep < 5 mmHg during retrohepatic and parenchymal dissection to minimize blood loss

---

## Local Resection vs. En Bloc Hepatectomy {.smaller}


- **Bile duct resection alone (local resection) is rarely adequate**


- **Indications for local resection (very select):**

    - No intrahepatic extension
    - No portal vein involvement
    - Must include: entire supraduodenal bile duct + gallbladder + cystic duct + extrahepatic hepatic ducts + supraduodenal tissue clearance + portal lymphadenectomy

- **MSKCC data (n=106):**

    - 19 local resections performed; 9 were R0
    - **Zero R0 local-resection patients were among 5-year survivors**

:::{.callout}
**Conclusion:** Local resections are associated with worse survival even with clear margins; en bloc hepatectomy is the preferred approach when technically feasible
:::

---

## ALPPS in Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma {.smaller}

**Associating Liver Partition and Portal Vein Ligation for Staged Hepatectomy**

- Two-stage: liver partition + portal vein ligation (stage 1) → rapid FLR hypertrophy → hepatectomy (stage 2)
- Perioperative morbidity: **80%** · Mortality: **12%**

:::{.callout-note}
**ALPPS is generally NOT recommended for HC:**

| Registry/Study | 90-Day Mortality |
|---|---|
| International ALPPS Registry (HC subset) | **27%** |
| ALPPS Italian Registry (biliary tumors) | **40%** |
| Matched case-control vs. standard resection | 48% vs. 24% |

Median survival: **6 months** (ALPPS) vs. **29 months** (standard resection)

Most HC patients have bactibilia → ↑ infectious risk + intraabdominal collections
:::

---

## Liver Transplantation for Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma {.smaller}

- **Historical results: dismal (2-yr OS ~48%; 50% recurrence within 2 years)**

- **Modern approach — Mayo Clinic HC Transplant Protocol:**

    - Neoadjuvant chemo + radiation + staging laparoscopy + lymph node assessment

- **Eligibility criteria:**

    - Mass lesion at biliary stricture, OR
    - Endoluminal tissue diagnosis, OR  
    - CA19-9 > 100
	
	
---

## Liver Transplantation for Hilar Cholangiocarcinoma {.smaller}

- **Contraindications:**

    - Tumor > 3 cm 
	- Positive nodes/metastases
	- Prior resection attempt
	- Transperitoneal biopsy
	- Previous malignancy

**Outcomes (Mayo, n=148 enrolled → 90 transplanted):**  
→ **75% 5-year overall survival**

:::{.callout-note}
**US EBM Consortium (n=304):** Transplant vs resection 5-yr OS: **64% vs 18%** (P<0.001)  
**TRANSPHIL trial (NCT02232932):** Ongoing RCT: transplant vs resection in resectable HC without PSC
:::

---

## Transplant vs. Resection — Current Guidance {.smaller}


- **When to resect:**
    - Resectable tumors where R0 is feasible → **resect**
    - No level 1 data demonstrating transplant superiority in resectable HC
    - Organ availability remains limited

- **When to refer for transplant:**
    - Unresectable locally advanced HC
    - HC in the setting of PSC
    - Highly selected patients meeting Mayo protocol criteria

---

## Transplant vs. Resection — Current Guidance

- **Caveats:**
    - ~1/3 of transplant candidates drop out pre-transplant (disease progression/death)
    - High incidence of occult lymph node and distant metastases limits applicability
    - Mayo group: no OS difference between transplant vs resection after adjusting for confounders

---

## Resection of Distal Cholangiocarcinoma{.smaller}

**Standard operation: Pancreatoduodenectomy (Whipple)**

:::{.callout-note}
**DC vs. pancreatic head adenocarcinoma:**

| Feature | Distal Cholangiocarcinoma | Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma |
|---|---|---|
| Resectability rate | **Higher** | Lower |
| Positive margins | **Less frequent** | More frequent |
| Lymph node involvement | **Less frequent** | More frequent |
:::


---

## Resection of Distal Cholangiocarcinoma{.smaller}

**Key prognostic factor:** Lymph node status

- Ethun et al.: lymph node involvement = **only independent predictor** of long-term survival in resected DC
- Positive nodes: **1.63× greater likelihood of death**

**Imaging clue for DC:** Dilated extrahepatic bile duct terminating abruptly at its distal aspect **without** a concomitantly dilated pancreatic duct → distal bile duct carcinoma

---

## Outcomes After Resection {.smaller}

- **5-Year survival after HC resection: 11–44%**  
- **Postoperative mortality: 4–17%**

| Study | n | Morbidity (%) | Mortality (%) | 5-yr Survival (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nakeeb 1996 | 109 | 47 | 4 | 11 |
| Klempnauer 1997 | 151 | NR | 10 | 28 |
| Neuhaus 1999 | 80 | 55 | 8 | 22 |
| Jarnagin 2005 | 106 | 50 | 7.5 | 40 |
| Igami 2010 | 298 | 43 | 2 | 42 |
| Nagino 2013 | 574 | 57 | 4.7 | 33 |
| Komaya 2018 | 402 | NR | NR | 43.7 |

---

## Outcomes After Resection {.smaller}


**Prognostic factors**:

- Margin status 
- Lymph node involvement 
- Tumor grade 
- Histology (papillary > nodular sclerosing)


---

## Recurrence After Resection {.smaller} 


- Recurrence occurs in **up to 75–76%** of patients after resection of HC


- **MSKCC single-institution review (n=404 R0 resections):**
    - 60% developed recurrence; recurrence ~50% at **10 years**

- **Multi-institutional analysis (n=306):**
    - 76% recurred after resection
    - \>25% recurred after **5 years of recurrence-free survival**
    - Node-positive disease → no recurrence-free survival beyond **7 years**

- **Pattern of recurrence:**
    - Distant metastases > locoregional recurrence after R0 resection
    - Isolated locoregional recurrence: up to **27%**
    - Common sites: locoregional, peritoneum, liver

---

## Adjuvant Therapy — Key Trials {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

**[BILCAP Trial]{.underline}** (UK, phase III)  
Adjuvant capecitabine vs. observation after R0/R1 resection

- n=447 (HC 29%, DC 35%, GB 18%, ICC 19%)
- Intention-to-treat: no significant difference (HR 0.81; P=0.097)
- **Per-protocol analysis:**  
  OS HR 0.75 (P=.03) · RFS HR 0.70 (P=.009) ✅
- **Practice-changing:** 6 months adjuvant capecitabine now standard
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**[PRODIGE 12 Trial]{.underline}** (France)  
GEMOX vs. surveillance (n=196, R0/R1)

- No difference in relapse-free survival  
  (HR 0.88; P=.48)
- Only 37% node-positive — may explain lack of benefit
- GEMOX not recommended

**BCAT Trial** (Japan, phase III)  
Adjuvant gemcitabine vs. observation (DC+HC, n=225)

- No significant difference in OS or RFS
:::
:::

---

## Adjuvant Therapy — Radiation & Ongoing Trials {.smaller}

**Adjuvant Radiation Therapy:**
    - Johns Hopkins reports: **no benefit** for adjuvant external beam or intraluminal radiation
    - Other series: possible benefit with positive hepatic duct margins

**SWOG S0809 (phase II, single arm):**
    - Adjuvant gem + cape → concurrent cape + RT (45 Gy to nodes; 54–59.4 Gy tumor bed)
    - 2-yr OS: **65%** (R0: 67%; R1: 60%)
    - Met prespecified endpoint but lacks comparison arm

---

## Palliative Therapy — Biliary Decompression {.smaller} 

- **Most HC patients are NOT suitable for resection**

- **Indications for palliative biliary decompression:**

    - Intractable pruritus
    - Cholangitis
    - Lowering bilirubin for chemotherapy eligibility
    - Recovering hepatic parenchymal function

:::{.callout}
**Jaundice alone (without pruritus or cholangitis) is NOT necessarily an indication for decompression in pure palliation setting**
:::


---

## Palliative Therapy — Biliary Decompression {.smaller}

**Stent comparison:**

| Type | Median Patency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Plastic stents | **1.4–3 months** | Initial approach; easier to exchange |
| Self-expanding metal stents (SEMS) | **~6 months** | Higher technical + functional success; fewer reinterventions |

- SEMS: technical success 98.8% vs plastic 88.3% (P<0.001)
- SEMS functional success: 97.9% vs 84.8% (P<0.001)

---

## Palliative Therapy — Segment III Bypass {.smaller}

**For patients found unresectable at exploration:**

:::{.callout}
**Segment III Bypass:**

- Most accessible intrahepatic biliary bypass
- Anastomosis placed at a distance from tumor → less prone to occlusion than SEMS
- Resolves jaundice in **~2/3** of HC patients
- Relief of jaundice in **70%** if functioning parenchyma is adequately drained
- Series of 55 bypasses: **80% 1-year patency; zero perioperative deaths** in HC group (n=20)
:::

---

## Palliative Therapy — Segment III Bypass

- **Caveats:**
    - Bypass to atrophic lobe or heavily tumor-involved lobe is **ineffective**
    - If undrained lobe has been percutaneously contaminated → risk of persistent biliary fistula and cholangitis
    - Right anterior or posterior sectoral ducts are alternatives to segment III

---

## Palliative Therapy — Systemic Chemotherapy {.smaller}

**ABC-02 Trial (n=410):**  

Cisplatin + gemcitabine vs. gemcitabine alone for locally advanced/metastatic biliary tract cancer

| Arm | Median OS |
|---|---|
| Gemcitabine alone | 8.2 months |
| Cisplatin + Gemcitabine | **11.7 months** |

:::{.callout}
**Gemcitabine + cisplatin = first-line standard of care** for unresectable/metastatic biliary tract cancers
:::

---

## Palliative Therapy — Systemic Chemotherapy {.smaller}

**Second-line chemotherapy:**

- Systematic review (n=761): insufficient evidence to recommend a specific regimen
- Further prospective randomized trials needed

**Radiation therapy:**

- External beam RT / SBRT: safe in well-selected patients
- Locally advanced without widespread disease
- Inappropriate in widespread metastatic disease

---

## Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) {.smaller}

**For unresectable hilar cholangiocarcinoma**

**Mechanism:**

1. Inject photosensitizing drug
2. Direct illumination via cholangioscopy with specific-wavelength light
3. Activation → reactive oxygen species → **tumor cell death**

**Evidence:**

- Two randomized studies: biliary stenting + PDT vs. biliary stenting alone  
  → **Improved survival** with combined approach

---

## Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) {.smaller}

:::{.callout}
**Why does PDT improve survival?**  
Likely due to **better biliary decompression** and avoidance of early segmental duct isolation/cholangitis — rather than significant tumor reduction
:::

Also used for: 

- esophagus 
- colon 
- stomach 
- bronchus 
- bladder 
- brain

---

## Targeted Therapy & Immunotherapy — Emerging Data {.smaller}

**Molecular drivers in EHC:**

- KRAS 55% · TP53 40% — common but not currently targetable
- **HER2 amplification: ~20%** of EHC → potential target
- ALK/TP53 mutations → worse prognosis
- **MMR deficiency: ~5%** → potential role for **immunotherapy** (pembrolizumab, etc.)
- Targetable mutations are **rare** in EHC vs. ICC (FGFR2, IDH in ICC are actionable)

:::{.callout}
**Current recommendations:**
- Molecular testing of EHC is **recommended** in all patients
- Genomic profiling to identify rare actionable alterations
- Growing interest in immune checkpoint inhibitors in MMR-deficient tumors
- Future: combination targeted therapy + immunotherapy
:::

---

## Summary & Key Takeaways {.smaller}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

**Diagnosis & Staging**

- MRCP has replaced direct cholangiography for initial staging
- Imaging **before** biliary decompression for accurate resectability assessment
- Tissue diagnosis not mandatory if clinical picture is clear
- Diagnostic laparoscopy avoids futile laparotomy in **~25%**
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Treatment**

- Resection = only curative option; requires R0 + en bloc hepatectomy ± caudate lobectomy
- Adjuvant capecitabine (6 months) — current standard post-resection
- Transplantation in selected unresectable HC or PSC-associated HC
- Gem + cisplatin: first-line palliation
:::
:::

:::{.callout}
**Future Directions:**

· Adjuvant strategies · Genomics · Epigenetics · Targeted therapies · Immunotherapy

— Interdisciplinary approach remains essential
:::
